Name: paraphrase_controlled_inconsistency
Title: Is Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Special? Using Within-Language Paraphrase Variation to Isolate the Language-Transition Component of Multilingual Factual Instability
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual factual inconsistency has two additive components: a language-agnostic instability that also causes a model to answer differently across paraphrases of the SAME language, and a genuinely language-specific instability introduced at the late-layer language-transition stage. We hypothesize (a) that a large, previously-unmeasured fraction of what is reported as 'cross-lingual inconsistency' is actually this baseline paraphrase instability rather than anything language-specific; (b) that the residual, language-specific component is causally localized to a distinct late-layer transition locus separable from the mid-layer concept computation; and (c) the size of the residual (not the total) is what scales with script/typological distance, while the paraphrase-baseline component does not.
Related Work: A wave of recent work attributes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a late-layer 'language transition' failure over a shared concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), and proposes fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubSub/SubInj, steering to a shared space). Separately, LLMs are known to be highly unstable to meaning-preserving surface changes WITHIN a language (Prompt-Format Sensitivity 2023; RoParQ 2025). Crucially, ALL cross-lingual consistency work compares one prompt per language and implicitly treats every observed disagreement as language-caused, never subtracting the model's baseline within-language paraphrase instability. No prior work measures the paraphrase-controlled residual, tests whether the celebrated 'language-transition' locus explains the residual specifically (rather than total inconsistency), or checks whether existing fixes reduce the residual or merely the paraphrase-baseline. We contribute this decomposition, a causal locus test on the residual, and a re-evaluation of prior interventions against the correct baseline. Our three pieces, ranked: (1) primary - a measurement correction showing a large share of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline within-language paraphrase instability; (2) a differential-localization result relocating the language-specific RESIDUAL, not total inconsistency, to a late-layer transition; (3) a re-evaluation of published fixes against the corrected baseline. We frame (2) as a differential-localization hypothesis rather than a strong single-locus causal claim.
Abstract: Multilingual language models give different factual answers to the same question asked in different languages, and a growing literature explains this via a late-layer 'language transition' over a shared, language-agnostic concept space. But these studies compare a single prompt per language and treat every disagreement as language-caused, ignoring that the same models also answer inconsistently across meaning-preserving paraphrases within a single language. We ask a sharp question: once we subtract this baseline paraphrase instability, how much cross-lingual inconsistency is genuinely language-specific, and is the language-transition mechanism responsible for that residual rather than for the total? We introduce a paraphrase-controlled decomposition: for each fact we measure within-language answer variability across multiple paraphrases in each language, and define the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement in excess of the pooled within-language baseline. Behaviorally, we predict a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline paraphrase noise, and that only the residual scales with script/typological distance. Mechanistically, we test whether the late-layer transition locus (via logit-lens and activation patching) causally explains the residual specifically: patching mid-layer concept representations should fix paraphrase-baseline errors in any language, whereas the residual should require correcting the late-layer transition. Finally we re-evaluate published fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubInj) against the correct baseline, testing whether they reduce the language-specific residual or merely the paraphrase-agnostic component. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B, sharpening what is and is not special about cross-lingual factual instability. Formally, for a fact f and language l we define within-language instability as the answer-disagreement rate across K paraphrases, and the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts minus the pooled within-language baseline; we test whether this decomposition is additive versus interaction-heavy with a hierarchical variance decomposition across fact, language, and paraphrase, so the residual is a well-identified estimand rather than a relabeling. The consequence is concrete: if total inconsistency is the wrong metric, multilingual QA leaderboards, model-release consistency claims, and factuality/safety audits should report the paraphrase-controlled residual, and practitioners should stop attributing paraphrase noise to language-specific failure.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, adapted): factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA (parallel templated facts; BMLAMA-53 supplies parallel items across 53 languages). Use 1,000 facts that exist in all chosen 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. For each fact in each language, generate K=5 meaning-preserving paraphrase templates, validated by back-translation and native-speaker spot checks; low-agreement paraphrases dropped and reported. This yields both within-language (across the 5 paraphrases) and cross-language variants for every fact. Per-language typological/script distance to the dominant language (English) from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + light patching, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Answer matching is alias-aware with answer-span normalization. 3 seeds (paraphrase sampling).

Experiment 1 (claim-a - how much cross-lingual inconsistency is really paraphrase baseline). Tests whether a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline within-language paraphrase instability. For each fact compute: (a) WITHIN-LANGUAGE instability = answer-disagreement rate across the 5 paraphrases within each language, averaged over languages; (b) TOTAL cross-lingual inconsistency = disagreement across languages using one canonical prompt each (matching prior single-prompt protocols); (c) LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC RESIDUAL = cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts minus the pooled within-language baseline. Decisive metric: the fraction of total inconsistency attributable to the paraphrase baseline vs the residual, per model. Convincing: the paraphrase baseline accounts for >= 30% of what the single-prompt protocol reports as cross-lingual inconsistency, in all three models, establishing that a substantial share is not language-specific. Indecision band: 15-30%; reported as a non-trivial but modest overcount. Negative result: baseline < 15% of total (cross-lingual inconsistency is overwhelmingly language-specific) refutes claim (a) - itself a clean, publishable vindication of the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline.

Experiment 2 (claim-c - only the residual scales with distance). Tests whether the language-specific residual, not the paraphrase baseline, tracks script/typological distance. Correlate each of (i) total inconsistency, (ii) paraphrase baseline, and (iii) residual with lang2vec typological/script distance to English. Decisive metric: Spearman of the residual with distance vs Spearman of the paraphrase baseline with distance (95% CIs). Convincing: the residual correlates with distance (Spearman >= 0.4) while the paraphrase baseline does not (|Spearman| < 0.2), and the total's apparent distance-dependence is driven by the residual. Indecision band: residual Spearman 0.2-0.4, or the baseline also correlating (0.2-0.4); reported as partial separation. Negative result: the paraphrase baseline correlating with distance as strongly as the residual, or the residual not correlating at all, refutes claim (c).

Experiment 3 (claim-b - concept vs late-layer transition locus by error type). Tests whether paraphrase-baseline errors are fixable at the mid-layer concept stage (any language) while the language-specific residual specifically requires correcting the late-layer transition. Replicate the mid-layer-concept / late-layer-transition split via logit lens per model first. For PARAPHRASE-BASELINE errors (a fact correct under one paraphrase, wrong under another, same language), patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct run into the wrong run and measure recovery. For RESIDUAL (language-specific) errors, test whether mid-layer concept patching alone recovers the answer or whether correcting the late-layer transition (a translation-difference / language-transition vector) is additionally required. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: recovery rate by error type and patch type. Convincing: paraphrase-baseline errors recover >= 50% from mid-layer concept patching regardless of language, while residual errors recover < 20% from concept patching alone but >= 50% once the late-layer transition is corrected. Indecision band: residual concept-patch recovery 20-40%; reported as a partially-shared locus. Negative result: residual errors recovering from mid-layer concept patching as well as baseline errors refutes the distinct-late-locus claim (b).

Experiment 4 (claim-b - locus separability). Tests that the components fixing paraphrase-baseline errors and those fixing residual errors are distinct. Quantify overlap (Jaccard) over the identified layers/heads/directions whose patching fixes each error type. Model frozen. Decisive metric: Jaccard overlap between the baseline-fixing and residual-fixing component sets. Convincing: Jaccard <= 0.3 (largely disjoint), with the residual-fixing set concentrated in later layers than the baseline-fixing set. Indecision band: Jaccard 0.3-0.5; reported as partial separability. Negative result: Jaccard > 0.5 (the same components fix both) refutes the separability claim.

Experiment 5 (claim-b - prior fixes act on the residual, corroborating the transition locus). Tests whether published cross-lingual-consistency fixes reduce the language-specific residual (as a language-transition intervention should) rather than merely the paraphrase baseline. Apply, faithfully re-implemented, the linear-shortcut (bypassing final layers), the translation-difference vector, and the English-subject-injection (SubInj) fixes; measure each fix's effect separately on the paraphrase baseline and on the residual. Model frozen except as each fix prescribes. Decisive metric: per-fix reduction of the residual vs reduction of the paraphrase baseline (percentage points). Convincing: at least one late-layer-targeted fix reduces the residual by >= 10 pp while leaving the paraphrase baseline largely unchanged (< 5 pp), showing the residual is the genuinely language-transition-addressable component. Indecision band: residual reduction 5-10 pp or comparable reduction of both components; reported as a general-robustness rather than transition-specific effect. Negative result: fixes reducing only the paraphrase baseline and not the residual would indicate they do not address a language-specific transition, qualifying claim (b).

Paraphrase quality and added controls. Beyond back-translation and native-speaker spot checks, a stratified subset receives bilingual human validation and automatic semantic-equivalence scoring, with robustness reported to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. We include multiple canonical prompts per language (not one), a translationese-vs-native paraphrase comparison, prompt-length and format matching, uncertainty intervals on every rate, and significance tests for all thresholded claims. The additivity of the decomposition is tested explicitly with a hierarchical (fact x language x paraphrase) variance model / ANOVA-style analysis reported alongside the point estimates.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Paraphrase quality across languages is uneven; low-quality paraphrases could inflate the within-language baseline and understate the residual. We validate paraphrases via back-translation and native-speaker checks and report sensitivity to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. 2. Answer matching across languages/scripts is noisy (aliases, transliterations); we use alias-aware matching and last-token/answer-span normalization and report robustness. 3. It is possible the paraphrase baseline is small and cross-lingual inconsistency IS mostly language-specific; this would refute claim (a) but is itself a valuable, publishable clarification that legitimizes the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline. 4. Logit-lens/patching localization may be diffuse; we report degree of localization honestly and require the recovery-by-error-type contrast (Exp. 4) rather than mere layer identification. 5. The concept-vs-transition split may not be crisp in all models; we validate it per model before the locus test. 6. Prior fixes may interact with our paraphrase set differently than their original setups; we replicate them faithfully and report both baseline and residual effects. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.
